Contents.Subtitle: Git user configs
Contents.Intro: When you regularly do work on computers that other users use.

Cheats.Explanation: Unset user.name and user.email from git globally and locally. Unsets only for the windows user that runs this command and the local repo, where this is run. Does not unset global configs of other windows users in the machine.
Cheats.Cheat:
git config --local --unset user.name
git config --local --unset user.email
git config --global --unset user.name
git config --global --unset user.email

Cheats.Explanation: Set your github user in your windows user globally.
Cheats.Cheat:
git config --global user.name 'MyGitHubUserName'
git config --global user.email 'my.email@address.com'

Cheats.Explanation: Edit commit author if you cannot set git config globally. This bypasses even the user config set in --local. Use this when you are not the only one with access to this machine.
Cheats.Cheat: git commit --author='Author Name <email@address.com>' -m '<Enter a commit message>'

Contents.Subtitle: Edit commit message
Contents.Intro: Small edits to commit messages. Amending the commit message changes the commit sha, thus amending pushed commits of branches edited simultaneously by multiple people will cause 'unrelated histories' merge conflicts.

Cheats.Cheat: git commit --amend -m '<insert the new commit message>'

Contents.Subtitle: 'Undo' bad commits
Contents.Intro: Recourse depend on whether the commit was pushed or not and if it was merge commit or regular commit.

Contents.Subtitle: Pushed commits
Contents.Intro: Pushed commits should not be literally 'undone'. Even when cleaning secrets from history.

Cheats.Explanation: Use revert to mark the commit as 'been-there-done-that-but-not-anymore'.
Cheats.Cheat: git revert -- <insert commit id you want to flip>

Cheats.Explanation:
If more than one commit (on same files) should be reverted, conflicts can be avoided by reverting in order of newest to oldest.
A revert commit can also be reverted later, if the changes are later reapplied.

Contents.Subtitle: Merge commits
Contents.Intro:
Merge commits are not regular commits. When a branch B is merged into a branch A, the commits from B will be introduced into history of A, along with a merge commit 'on top' of it all.
Therefore it may take longer time to address bad merge commits. The solution also depends on whether the merge was pushed or not and if the changes included by the merge are in branches actively worked on.

Contents.Subtitle: Unpushed merge
Contents.Intro: If the merge was not pushed and nothing (meaningful) was changed after the merge, most likely 'reset' works fine.

Contents.Subtitle: Pushed merge
Contents.Intro: It gets complicated if the merge was pushed. Revert should be preferred for pushed changes, but 'revert' is not actually the same as 'undo' or ctrl+Z like stated earlier.

Cheats.Explanation:
In the case of a merge commit, 'revert' states that all the commits from the source branch are abandoned. Because merging also copies the commits from the other branch, reverting a merge marks those too as abandoned. So, if a branch containing commits from the branch B is later directly merged back to the branch A, those commits will remain abandoned. If this is not the purpose, the merge revert or the simultaneously revert commits should be (re-)reverted before a new merge.
In addition to complicating merges in the future, reverting a merge also requires bit more flags to state the commit to return to. Because with merge, you have two viable options: The latest commit of the branch A or the branch B before the merge.
Cheats.Cheat: git revert -m 1/2 <insert commit you want to get to in the parent branch>

You want to merge two branches, both of which includes changes made after split. However, you do not want the end result to have any active changes from one of the branches while both should be visible in commit history. Kind of like moving one branch to trash bin but never fully deleting it. Use 'ours' or 'theirs' to indicate the branch which you want to 'keep active'.
